(c) [3:365] Compare—(nonstandard) policy covering “accident or event”: The result may be different where a liability policy defines “occurrence” as an “accident or event” causing bodily injury or property damage. Such a provision may require the insurer to defend a wrongful discharge suit because “event” may include nonaccidental (i.e., intentional) acts. [United Pac. Ins. Co. v. McGuire Co. (1991) 229 CA3d 1560, 1565-1567, 281 CR 375, 378-379—potential coverage for damages for mental distress from wrongful termination] 1) [3:365.1] Does not include “wilful” acts: As a matter of law, there can be no coverage for “wilful acts” (Ins.C. § 533; see discussion at ¶ 3:105 ff.). Therefore, despite coverage for intentional acts, there is no coverage for any injury or damage expected or intended by the insured: “[T]he defendants were covered for the intentional act of terminating the plaintiff, as long as the result of the termination—i.e., emotional distress—was not intended by the defendants.” [Waller v.
